parts.label: (a)
hints: Hint 1: Think about what an X-ray film looks like - some parts are dark and some are light, so what does good contrast mean for telling two neighbouring regions apart?
parts.proper_answer: Contrast is the difference in the degree of blackening between different parts of the X-ray image.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Picture What You See On The Film**
Imagine holding an X-ray up to the light. Bone looks white, soft tissue looks grey, air looks black. You can tell structures apart because one area is darker than another. That visible difference is all contrast means.

Step 2: **State It Simply**
So contrast is just how much darker or lighter one region is compared to another. In physics terms, it is the difference in degrees of blackening on the image.

parts.label: (b)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Look at Fig. 10.1 and follow a ray in region B - which material does it go through only, and what total thickness does it travel through?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Sort Out The Path In Region B**
In region B the beam misses material Q completely. It travels only through material P. From the diagram the total thickness of P there is $x = 5.8 \text{ cm}$ and $\mu = 0.35 \text{ cm}^{-1}$.

Step 2: **Apply Exponential Attenuation**
X-ray intensity falls off exponentially:
$$I = I_0 \exp(-\mu x)$$
Put the numbers in before calculating:
$$I = I_0 \exp(-0.35 \times 5.8) = I_0 \exp(-2.03)$$
$$I \approx 0.13 I_0$$
That is the required result.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Follow a ray in region A - it passes through both P and Q, so what thickness of each material does it travel through if the total width is 5.8 cm and Q is 2.1 cm wide?
Hint 2: Think how to combine two attenuations in series - the beam is reduced by P then reduced again by Q, so the exponents add together in a single exponential expression.
Hint 3: You know the final intensity is $0.053I_0$, so set up the equation and take natural logs to isolate the unknown $\mu$ for Q.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Work Out The Two Thicknesses**
In region A the beam goes through Q of thickness $x_Q = 2.1 \text{ cm}$ plus the rest of P. Total width is $5.8 \text{ cm}$, so thickness of P is:
$$x_P = 5.8 - 2.1 = 3.7 \text{ cm}$$

Step 2: **Write The Combined Attenuation**
Attenuation by P multiplies attenuation by Q, so exponents add:
$$I_A = I_0 \exp(-\mu_P x_P) \times \exp(-\mu_Q x_Q) = I_0 \exp{-[\mu_P x_P + \mu_Q x_Q]}$$
With $I_A = 0.053 I_0$:
$$0.053 I_0 = I_0 \exp{-[(0.35 \times 3.7) + 2.1\mu]}$$

parts.label: (b)(iii)
hints: Hint 1: Compare your two transmitted intensities, $0.13I_0$ for B and $0.053I_0$ for A - how big is the ratio between them and what does that mean for the difference in blackening?
parts.proper_answer: The detected intensities differ by a factor of only about 2.5 ($0.13/0.053$), so the difference in blackening is small and contrast is poor.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link Intensities To Contrast**
Remember from (a), contrast is difference in blackening, and blackening depends on detected intensity. Here:
$$I_B = 0.13 I_0 \text{ and } I_A = 0.053 I_0$$
The ratio is:
$$\frac{I_B}{I_A} = \frac{0.13}{0.053} \approx 2.5$$
That is only a small factor, so the two regions will blacken the film by similar amounts and will be hard to tell apart. That is poor contrast.

parts.label: (c)
hints: Hint 1: A normal X-ray squashes all depth into one flat shadow, so how could you avoid overlap by looking at just one thin slice at a time?
Hint 2: One view through a slice is not enough to locate a small object inside it, so why would rotating the X-ray tube and detector around the slice and taking many views help?
Hint 3: Once you have mapped one slice, how do you build up the full volume - what must be repeated and combined?
parts.proper_answer: The structure is scanned in thin sections. Many scans of each section are taken from different angles. Scanning is repeated for all sections and the data are compiled by computer to form a 3D image.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Slice Into Thin Sections**
Instead of one picture through the whole body, CT uses a narrow, collimated X-ray beam to view just one thin cross-sectional slice. This removes confusion from structures above and below.

Step 2: **Scan From Many Angles**
The X-ray tube and detectors rotate around that slice, taking many attenuation measurements from different angles. A computer uses all these different projections to work out the attenuation at each point within the slice and build a 2D image of that slice.

Step 3: **Stack Slices Into 3D**
The patient is moved slightly and the process is repeated for the next slice, until all slices covering the volume are done. The computer then compiles all the slice images together to produce a full three-dimensional image of the internal structure.
